title: Farfus wins at Zandvoort as Rockenfeller clinches the 2013 title
dek: Augusto Farfus won by 1.603 seconds from Mike Rockenfeller, whose second place made him champion with one race still to run.

chapters.title: One more finish for Rockenfeller
text: The ninth of ten races of the 2013 DTM took the series to Zandvoort on Sunday 29 September, two weeks after Augusto Farfus had won at Oschersleben from Mike Rockenfeller and Jamie Green. That result left Rockenfeller leading the championship on 124 points, 33 clear of Farfus on 91, with Christian Vietoris on 71, Robert Wickens on 70, Bruno Spengler on 67 and Gary Paffett on 65 behind them. Only 50 points remained available, so the title had become a duel between the Audi driver and the BMW driver.

The arithmetic was unforgiving for Farfus. He needed to take at least eight points out of Rockenfeller in the Netherlands to keep the fight alive for the Hockenheim finale, and even a win would not be enough if Rockenfeller finished second: 25 points against 18 would leave the gap at 26, one more than the finale could give back. Rockenfeller, who had scored in every race so far, was therefore one good finish away from the title.
The race rewarded strategy as much as speed. Zandvoort's dunes offered little room to overtake, which made track position at the pit stops all the more valuable.

chapters.title: Wittmann takes a first pole, Mercedes struggles
text: Marco Wittmann, 23 and in his first DTM season with the new BMW Team MTEK, took his first DTM pole with a 1:30.894 in the final shoot-out. He was first onto the track in that session and then watched Timo Scheider and Farfus fail to beat the time. Farfus, who had looked the favourite after a strong Saturday, was 0.085 seconds slower in second on the grid, and Rockenfeller took third with a 1:31.325. Scheider, who made a mistake on his lap, was fourth.

Joey Hand put the second RBM BMW fifth, ahead of Filipe Albuquerque and Edoardo Mortara in the Rosberg Audis, with Timo Glock eighth in the other MTEK car. Adrien Tambay and Miguel Molina were ninth and tenth. Mattias Ekström missed the top ten and started 11th, with Paffett 12th as the best of the Mercedes.

It was a poor session for Mercedes. Vietoris, like the Audi of Green, was eliminated in the first segment, and the two lined up 16th and 17th once Spengler, who qualified 16th, dropped two places to 18th for the accident with Wickens at Oschersleben. Daniel Juncadella, Wickens and Roberto Merhi filled the last three places, and Wickens' hopes had ended in the first session when he put two wheels on the grass at the Arie Luyendijkbocht on his final run.

chapters.title: Farfus and Rockenfeller jump pole-sitter Wittmann
text: In sunshine and around 15 degrees, Farfus made the cleaner getaway and was ahead of Wittmann by the first corner. Rockenfeller also got past the pole-sitter and settled into second, but the stewards looked at his start for a possible jump. They took no action and he kept the place.

Farfus used the pace of his RBM-run BMW to open a lead of around four seconds before the first stops, with Rockenfeller pushing hard on the softer Hankook option, where the Audi was at its best. Merhi, who started last, was out on the very first lap.

chapters.title: Farfus covers the Audi and pulls away on the standard tyre
text: Farfus pitted first, on lap 13, and Rockenfeller followed on lap 15, which meant that the BMW rejoined still in front. On the standard tyre Farfus stretched his lead to around 15 seconds. He said afterwards that the option tyres had faded and Rockenfeller had closed right up in the first stint, but that the car was better on the harder compound and he could then pull clear. On lap 31 the gap was 12.775 seconds.

Rockenfeller found the standard tyre difficult. Scheider ran close behind him, and Rockenfeller was glad to have a fellow Audi driver covering his rear. Behind them, Paffett opted for an aggressive early double stop in the hope of gaining track position, which worked at first but left him short of grip at the end of a long final stint, and Pascal Wehrlein, who had switched to the standard tyre early, spent the final 15 laps defending against rivals on fresher options.

chapters.title: Green and Werner collide, the field bunches up
text: With Farfus controlling the race, the late stages were reshaped by the collision between Green and Dirk Werner at the Arie Luyendijkbocht. Werner's BMW ended up in the gravel and the safety car came out, erasing the lead that Farfus had built and packing the field together for the restart. Green said afterwards that the two had touched and that he was unable to catch up again after his own semi-spin; he took the flag 13th. Werner was classified 21st, seven laps down.

The delay suited the drivers who had saved their option tyres. Ekström, who started 11th, had fitted the soft compound for his last stint and moved from seventh to fourth on the final lap. Tambay, who finished sixth, said the safety car had spoiled a chance of fourth for him.

chapters.title: Farfus wins by 1.603s; Rockenfeller second and champion
text: Farfus completed the 44 laps in 1:13:26.294 and crossed the line 1.603 seconds ahead of Rockenfeller, who took the flag as champion. Scheider was third, 2.149 seconds back, his best result of a difficult season. Ekström was fourth, 3.383 seconds behind the winner, after climbing from 11th on the grid.

Wittmann, who had started from pole, finished fifth, 3.652 seconds behind, and also set the fastest lap, a 1:32.296 on lap six. Tambay was sixth and Hand seventh, ahead of Albuquerque in eighth. Paffett was the best of the Mercedes drivers in ninth, 6.795 seconds back, and Molina completed the points in tenth. Martin Tomczyk was 11th and Wehrlein 12th.

It was a rough afternoon for the other BMWs. Glock fell from eighth on the grid to 18th, Andy Priaulx was 19th, and Spengler, who started 18th, finished 20th, 21.301 seconds behind the winner. Werner was classified 21st after the collision and Merhi was the only driver to retire.

chapters.title: A title wrapped up with a race to spare
text: Farfus took his third win of the season, his second in a row, and said he could not have done any better. He admitted the race had been harder than it looked, with his tyres dropping off in the first stint, and congratulated Rockenfeller on a deserved title. The win secured him second place in the drivers' standings, now beyond reach on 116 points.

Rockenfeller's 142 points settled the championship in Holland, with one race to spare, after he had scored in all nine races. He said he needed a few minutes to take it in, that the start had added some spice to a long race, and that he had briefly dreamed of victory when he closed on Farfus before the standard tyre gave him trouble. Audi's DTM head Dieter Gass said the team had not expected to be able to wrap up the title that day, and put the result down to calm work on the option tyres, as shown by Ekström. Scheider said it felt especially good to have helped him.

For Mercedes it was a weekend to forget. Paffett's ninth place was the best of the five cars that finished, and the head of DTM management, Wolfgang Schattling, said that qualifying had cost the team its chance of a result. BMW's motorsport director Jens Marquardt called Farfus's drive sensational, conceded that the way the race ended had not helped his side, and said BMW would still go for the manufacturers' and team titles in the finale. Vietoris stayed third in the standings on 71 points, one ahead of Wickens, with Paffett and Spengler both on 67. The team fight was just as tight: Audi Sport Team Phoenix led on 151 points, three ahead of BMW Team RBM on 148 and ten ahead of the best Mercedes team on 141, while Audi held a narrow lead over BMW in the manufacturers' table.
Those battles, and the question of who would finish third among the drivers, were left to the finale at Hockenheim on Sunday 20 October, three weeks later.

facts.t: Title with a race to spare
facts.v: Mike Rockenfeller finished second and moved to 142 points, 26 ahead of Augusto Farfus, more than the 25 available at the Hockenheim finale.
